title: Ragtime in New Orleans
summary: Hug and Allen discuss whether ragtime was played in New Orleans; Hug stresses the blues in saloons.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Now, was ragtime the popular style piano then? Would you say that?

Well, I would say to a great extent they were playing things around here that sounded like ragtime. Yeah, I guess there were many piano players, and as a matter of fact, I know Dick can discuss this a lot better than I can because he's gone into this and researched it, all that sort of thing. My feelings, my feelings is that ragtime is basically not in the wall of music. Is that right now? I mean, although it might have been played here, we might have played it.
Yeah, it seems to me that it came here from another place. I think, didn't it? And there was some ragtime performances here, but I'd have shut the door. Thank the Lord.
Well, I'm glad we're getting some privacy now.
Well, yeah, tell us a little bit about that. No, no. You know a little bit more about that than I do. Maybe I may be wrong in saying that, how did I play that?
They played it here, but they played a lot of other things, and you remember what they played.

I think, John, that I would say that ragtime was something that was a syncopated kind of music that was started, where it started at, I couldn't truthfully say. They say that a lot of people say it started up in St. Louis, a lot of people say it started in various other parts, but I don't know. I couldn't say that. But I guess probably that, as Dick says, it drifted... If it did start somewhere else, naturally, it would be only natural that the musicians here would have picked up on it to a certain extent. But I might add this, John, that to my knowledge, the musicians here that played music when I came were not playing just ragtime. They were playing a lot of other things besides ragtime. And I would say that this makes... This is where the difference came in. That in New Orleans, I think you could go and walk down the street, you'd hear some piano player in a saloon playing blues on some old beat-up piano. But it was a real great sound, you know, just a slow blues. You couldn't put your finger on it. You couldn't tell what it was. I couldn't tell you right now what they were playing, but you could tell it was something real good. And that's what I think is making New Orleans.
